nodes.statement: Recall that a $k G$-module is projective if and only if it is injective. We write $\mathsf{StMod}(k G)$ for the stable category of $k G$-modules, and $\mathsf{stmod}(k G)$ for the full subcategory of finitely generated $k G$-modules. These are triangulated categories in which the graded homomorphisms from $M$ to $N$ are the Tate groups $\mathsf{E\widehat{\phantom{\dot{}}x}t}^*_{k G}(M,N)$. Recall also that $\hat H^i(G,M)$ denotes $\mathsf{E\widehat{\phantom{\dot{}}x}t}^i_{k G}(k,M)$.
nodes.name: Stable module category StMod(kG)
nodes.statement_short: StMod(kG) is the stable module category, stmod(kG) its finitely generated part; morphisms are Tate Ext groups.
also_stated_at: We write $\mathsf{StMod}(k G)$ for the stable category of $k G$-modules, a compactly generated triangulated category whose compact objects $\mathsf{stmod}(k G)$ consist of the thick subcategory of modules stably isomorphic to finitely generated modules.

nodes.statement: If $M$ and $N$ are $k G$-modules, we say that a homomorphism $M \to N$ is a \emph{cohomology equivalence} if the induced map $\hat H^*(G,M) \to \hat H^*(G,N)$ is an isomorphism, or equivalently if $\hat H^{\geqslant 0}(G,M) \to \hat H^{\geqslant 0}(G,N)$ is an isomorphism, see Proposition~\ref{pr:gaps} and Corollary~\ref{co:gaps} below. This is not an equivalence relation, but we complete it to one. Note that we do not require this to hold for subgroups of $G$. We say that $M$ and $N$ are cohomologically equivalent if they are equivalent with respect to this equivalence relation. In other words, there is a zig-zag of cohomological equivalences relating $M$ and $N$. We say that $M$ is a \emph{no cohomology module} if the Tate cohomology $\hat H^*(G,M)=0$, or equivalently if $\hat H^{\geqslant 0}(G,M)=0$.
nodes.name: Cohomology equivalence; no cohomology module
nodes.statement_short: A map is a cohomology equivalence if it induces an isomorphism on Tate cohomology; cohomological equivalence is the generated equivalence relation; no cohomology modules have zero Tate cohomology.
also_stated_at: If $M$ and $N$ are $k G$-modules, we say that a homomorphism $M \to N$ is a \emph{cohomology equivalence} if the induced map on Tate cohomology is an isomorphism. This is not an equivalence relation, but we complete it to one, and then talk of $M$ and $N$ being cohomologically equivalent. We say that $M$ is a \emph{no cohomology module} if its Tate cohomology vanishes.

nodes.statement: Suppose that $G$ is a finite $p$-group. If $M$ is a $k G$-module such that $H^0(G,M)$ is finite dimensional then $M$ is finitely generated. If $\hat H^n(G,M)$ is finite dimensional for some $n\in\mathbb Z$ then $M$ is a direct sum of a finite dimensional module and a projective module, and hence equivalent to a finite dimensional module in the stable module category.

conclusions: $M$ is finitely generated

nodes.statement: Recall that for a finite $p$-group in characteristic $p$, there is only one simple module, namely the trivial $k G$-module $k$. Its projective cover and injective hull are both $k G$, and every injective is a direct sum of copies of $k G$. Let $I$ be the injective hull of $M$. Then the inclusion $M \to I$ induces an isomorphism $H^0(G,M) \to H^0(G,I)$. But $I$ is a direct sum of copies of $k G$, so the dimension of $I$ is $|G|.\dim H^0(G,I)$. So if $H^0(G,M)$ is finite dimensional then $I$ is finite dimensional, and hence so is $M$. Similarly, if $\hat H^n(G,M)$ is finite dimensional with $n\in\mathbb Z$ then in a minimal Tate resolution $\cdots \to I_{-1} \to I_0 \to I_1\to \cdots$ of $M$, the dimension of $I_n$ is $|G|.\dim\hat H^n(G,M)$, and so the dimension of $\Omega^{-n}M$ is finite. Finally, $M$ is a direct sum of $\Omega^n\Omega^{-n}M$ and a projective module.
nodes.statement_short: Injective hulls over a $p$-group are sums of copies of $kG$, so dimension is $|G|$ times the dimension of fixed points; apply to $M$ and to a minimal Tate resolution.

nodes.statement: Recall that $H^n(G,M)$ agrees with $\hat H^n(G,M)$ for $n>0$. In degree zero, we have a surjective map $H^0(G,M) \to \hat H^0(G,M)$ whose kernel is the ``projective'' fixed points of $M$, namely the image of $\sum_{g\in G}g \in k G$ on $M$. Expressing $M$ as a direct sum of a projective module $P$ and a module $M'$ with no projective summands, the kernel is the fixed points of $G$ on $P$ and the image is the fixed points of $G$ on $M'$. Combining this with Proposition~\ref{pr:gaps}, we see that if $H^*(G,M)=0$ then $\hat H^*(G,M)=0$, and that if $\hat H^*(G,M)=0$ then $H^*(G,M)$ is concentrated in degree zero. Similarly, if $H^*(G,M)$ is finitely generated as a module over $H^*(G,k)$ then $\hat H^{\geqslant 0}(G,M)$ is also finitely generated, while if $\hat H^{\geqslant 0}(G,M)$ is finitely generated then $M$ is a direct sum of a projective module $P$ and a module $M'$ such that $H^*(G,M')$ is finitely generated. So we may as well work in the stable module category, which means that we should ignore projective summands.
nodes.name: Ordinary versus Tate cohomology in degree zero
nodes.statement_short: Compares $H^*$ and $\hat H^*$: they differ only by projective summands in degree zero, so one can work in the stable module category.

nodes.statement: We have a recollement of triangulated categories \[ \xymatrix{k^\perp \ar[r]|(0.4)u & \mathsf{StMod}(k G) \ar[r]|(0.45)v\ar@<1ex>[l]^(0.6){u_\lambda}\ar@<-1ex>[l]_(0.6){u_\rho} & \mathsf{StMod}(k G)/k^\perp \ar@<1ex>[l]^(0.55){v_\lambda} \ar@<-1ex>[l]_(0.55){v_\rho},} \] where the right hand side is the Verdier quotient.
nodes.name: Recollement for k-perp in StMod(kG)

nodes.statement: $\mathsf{StMod}^b(k G)$ is a thick subcategory of $\mathsf{StMod}(k G)$.
nodes.name: StMod^b(kG) is thick
conclusions: $\mathsf{StMod}^b(k G)$ is a thick subcategory of $\mathsf{StMod}(k G)$.

nodes.statement: $\mathsf{StMod}^b(k G)$ is clearly closed under direct summands. It follows from part (2) of Proposition~\ref{pr:gaps} that $M$ is in $\mathsf{StMod}(kG)$ if and only if $\Omega(M)$ is, and then the long exact sequence in cohomology shows that it is a triangulated subategory.
nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.20
nodes.statement_short: Closure under summands is clear; part (2) of Proposition 2.14 gives closure under $\Omega$ and the long exact sequence gives triangles.

nodes.statement: If $M$ is in $\mathsf{StMod}^b(k G)$ then so is the dual $M^\vee$.
nodes.name: Duality preserves StMod^b
conclusions: so is the dual $M^\vee$
nodes.label: pr:dual

nodes.statement: We examine the local cohomology spectral sequence~\cite{Greenlees:1995a} \[ E_2^{s,t}=(H^{s}_{\mathfrak{m}} H^*(G,M))^t \Rightarrow H_{-s-t}(G,M). \] By definition of Tate cohomology, the right hand side is $\hat H^{s+t-1}(G,M)$ when $s+t\leqslant 0$. Now suppose that $H^*(G,M)$ is finitely generated as a module over $H^*(G,k)$. Then the $E_2$ term is Artinian as a module over $H^*(G,k)$, and hence so are $H_*(G,M)$ and $\hat H^{\leqslant 0}(G,M)$. In particular, it is finite dimensional in each degree. So by Tate duality, this is a shift of the graded dual of $H^*(G,M^\vee)$ as $H^*(G,k)$-modules. So the latter is Noetherian as a graded module over $H^*(G,k)$.
nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.21
nodes.statement_short: Local cohomology spectral sequence: finitely generated cohomology gives Artinian homology, which by Tate duality is dual to the cohomology of $M^\vee$.

nodes.name: Local cohomology spectral sequence
nodes.statement_short: Set up the local cohomology spectral sequence converging to Tate cohomology in negative degrees.

nodes.name: Artinian abutment
nodes.statement_short: Finite generation makes $E_2$, hence negative Tate cohomology, Artinian.

nodes.statement: In particular, it is finite dimensional in each degree. So by Tate duality, this is a shift of the graded dual of $H^*(G,M^\vee)$ as $H^*(G,k)$-modules.
nodes.name: Tate duality
nodes.statement_short: Degreewise finite, so Tate duality identifies it with the dual of $H^*(G,M^\vee)$.

nodes.statement: So the latter is Noetherian as a graded module over $H^*(G,k)$.
nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement_short: Hence $H^*(G,M^\vee)$ is Noetherian.

nodes.statement: Suppose that a $k G$-module $M$ has no projective summands. Then neither does the dual $M^\vee=\mathsf{Hom}_k(M,k)$.
nodes.name: Duals of modules without projective summands
assumptions: a $k G$-module $M$ has no projective summands
conclusions: neither does the dual $M^\vee=\mathsf{Hom}_k(M,k)$
nodes.label: le:dual

nodes.statement: The problem we have to contend with here is that the kernel of the action of $k G$ on the dual $M^\vee$ is not the same as the kernel of the action on $M$, because of the intervention of the antipode $\sigma\colon k G\to k G$, $\sigma(g)=g^{-1}$, in the definition of the dual. One way to get around this is to consider the double dual $M^{\vee\vee}\cong M^{**}$. Since $\sigma^2$ is the identity, the natural inclusion $M \to M^{\vee\vee}$ does not involve the antipode, and the annihilators of $M$ and $M^{\vee\vee}$ are equal. Since $kG$ is self-injective, a module $M$ has no projective summands if and only if the socle of the group algebra $\mathsf{Soc}(k G)$ acts as zero on $M$. If this holds then $\mathsf{Soc}(k G)$ also acts as zero on $M^{\vee\vee}$, so $M^{\vee\vee}$ has no projective summands. On the other hand, the dual of a projective module is projective, so if $M^\vee$ has a projective summand then so does $M^{\vee\vee}$.
nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.22
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the double dual to avoid the antipode; no projective summands iff the socle of $kG$ acts as zero.

One way to get around this is to consider the double dual $M^{\vee\vee}\cong M^{**}$.
nodes.name: Antipode issue; pass to double dual
nodes.statement_short: The antipode changes the kernel of the action; consider the double dual instead.

nodes.statement: Since $\sigma^2$ is the identity, the natural inclusion $M \to M^{\vee\vee}$ does not involve the antipode, and the annihilators of $M$ and $M^{\vee\vee}$ are equal.
nodes.name: Double dual has same annihilator
nodes.statement_short: $\sigma^2=1$ so $M$ and $M^{\vee\vee}$ have equal annihilators.

nodes.statement: Since $kG$ is self-injective, a module $M$ has no projective summands if and only if the socle of the group algebra $\mathsf{Soc}(k G)$ acts as zero on $M$.
nodes.name: Socle criterion
nodes.statement_short: No projective summands iff the socle of $kG$ acts as zero.

nodes.statement: If this holds then $\mathsf{Soc}(k G)$ also acts as zero on $M^{\vee\vee}$, so $M^{\vee\vee}$ has no projective summands.
nodes.name: Apply criterion to double dual
nodes.statement_short: So $M^{\vee\vee}$ has no projective summands.

nodes.statement: On the other hand, the dual of a projective module is projective, so if $M^\vee$ has a projective summand then so does $M^{\vee\vee}$.
nodes.name: Conclude for M^vee
nodes.statement_short: A projective summand of $M^\vee$ would give one of $M^{\vee\vee}$.

nodes.statement: For $M$ in $\mathsf{StMod}^b(k G)$, the natural map to the double dual \[ M \to M^{**} \cong M^{\vee\vee} \] is a cohomology isomorphism.
nodes.name: Double dual is a cohomology isomorphism
conclusions: the natural map to the double dual \[ M \to M^{**} \cong M^{\vee\vee} \] is a cohomology isomorphism
nodes.label: pr:double-dual

nodes.statement: We may suppose without loss of generality that $\Omega^{-i}M$ has no projective summands. Then by Lemma~\ref{le:dual}, nor does $(\Omega^{-i}M)^*$ or $(\Omega^{-i}M)^{**}=(\Omega^iM^*)^*$, so we may take \[ \Omega^{-i}(M^{**})=(\Omega^iM^*)^*=(\Omega^{-i}M)^{**}. \] So \[ \mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(k,\Omega^{-i}(M^{**})) \cong (\mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(\Omega^iM^*,k))^* \cong (\mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(k,\Omega^{-i}M))^{**}. \] Then since there are no projective summands, we have $\mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(k,\Omega^{-i}M) \cong \hat H^i(G,M)$. In particular, if $\hat H^i(G,M)$ is finite dimensional then the map \[ \hat H^i(G,M)\to \hat H^i(G,M^{**})\cong \hat H^i(G,M)^{**} \] is an isomorphism as required.
nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.23
nodes.statement_short: Remove projective summands using Lemma 2.22, then identify Tate cohomology of the double dual with the double dual of Tate cohomology, finite dimensional in each degree.

nodes.statement: We may suppose without loss of generality that $\Omega^{-i}M$ has no projective summands.
nodes.name: WLOG no projective summands
nodes.statement_short: Assume $\Omega^{-i}M$ has no projective summands.

nodes.statement: Then by Lemma~\ref{le:dual}, nor does $(\Omega^{-i}M)^*$ or $(\Omega^{-i}M)^{**}=(\Omega^iM^*)^*$, so we may take \[ \Omega^{-i}(M^{**})=(\Omega^iM^*)^*=(\Omega^{-i}M)^{**}. \]
nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2.22
nodes.statement_short: Duals also lack projective summands, identifying $\Omega^{-i}(M^{**})$.

nodes.statement: So \[ \mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(k,\Omega^{-i}(M^{**})) \cong (\mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(\Omega^iM^*,k))^* \cong (\mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(k,\Omega^{-i}M))^{**}. \]
nodes.name: Hom computation
nodes.statement_short: Compute fixed points of $\Omega^{-i}(M^{**})$ as a double dual.

nodes.statement: Then since there are no projective summands, we have $\mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(k,\Omega^{-i}M) \cong \hat H^i(G,M)$.
nodes.name: Identify with Tate cohomology
nodes.statement_short: Fixed points equal Tate cohomology.

nodes.statement: In particular, if $\hat H^i(G,M)$ is finite dimensional then the map \[ \hat H^i(G,M)\to \hat H^i(G,M^{**})\cong \hat H^i(G,M)^{**} \] is an isomorphism as required.
nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement_short: Finite dimensional groups equal their double duals.

nodes.statement: If there is a counterexample to Conjecture~\ref{conj:strong-stmod} then there is a pure injective counterexample.
nodes.name: Pure injective counterexamples
assumptions: there is a counterexample to Conjecture~\ref{conj:strong-stmod}
conclusions: there is a pure injective counterexample

nodes.statement: This follows from Proposition~\ref{pr:double-dual}, since a module is pure injective if and only if it is isomorphic to a direct summand of the dual of a module.
nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.24
nodes.statement_short: By Proposition 2.23 and the characterisation of pure injectives as summands of duals.

nodes.statement: Let $\mathsf{KInj}(k G)$ be the homotopy category of complexes of injective $k G$-modules. This is a tensor triangulated category. Its tensor identity $\mathsf{ik}$ is an injective resolution of $k$ as a $k G$-module. We also write $\mathsf{pk}$ for a projective resolution of $k$ and $\mathsf{tk}$ for a Tate resolution of $k$. These sit in a triangle \[ \mathsf{pk} \to \mathsf{ik} \to \mathsf{tk} \to \Sigma\mathsf{pk}. \] Note that we index objects in $\mathsf{KInj}(k G)$ cohomologically, so that $\mathsf{ik}$ lives in positive degrees while $\mathsf{pk}$ lives in negative degrees. As a result, the endomorphism rings of $\mathsf{ik}$ and $\mathsf{pk}$, which are both the cohomology ring, live in positive degree. If $X$ is an object in $\mathsf{KInj}(k G)$, we write \[ H^*(G,X) = \mathsf{Hom}^*_{\mathsf{KInj}(k G)}(\mathsf{ik},X)\cong H^*(\mathsf{Hom}^*_{k G}(k,X)). \]
nodes.name: Homotopy category KInj(kG)
nodes.statement_short: KInj(kG) is the homotopy category of complexes of injectives, with tensor unit ik, projective and Tate resolutions pk, tk, and cohomology $H^*(G,X)$.
also_stated_at: We write $\mathsf{KInj}(k G)$ for the homotopy category of complexes of injective $k G$-modules, studied in~\cite{Benson/Krause:2008a}.

nodes.statement: Its compact objects are the semi-injective resolutions of finite complexes of finitely generated $k G$-modules, and these form a thick subcategory equivalent to the bounded derived category $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$.
nodes.name: Compact objects of KInj(kG) are D^b(kG)
conclusions: Its compact objects are the semi-injective resolutions of finite complexes of finitely generated $k G$-modules, and these form a thick subcategory equivalent to the bounded derived category $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$
also_stated_at: The thick subcategory of compact objects in $\mathsf{KInj}(k G)$ is equivalent to $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$ via semi-injective resolutions, and we identify it with $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$.

nodes.statement: Every complex $X$ of injective $k G$-modules is a direct sum of a split exact sequence of injectives and a complex $Y$ that is \emph{minimal} in the sense that the socle in each degree is in the kernel of the differential.
nodes.name: Minimal complex of injectives
differentia: the socle in each degree is in the kernel of the differential

nodes.statement: For a minimal complex $X$ we have $H^n(G,X)\cong \mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(k,X^n)$.
nodes.name: Cohomology of a minimal complex
conclusions: $H^n(G,X)\cong \mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(k,X^n)$

nodes.statement: We have an embedding of $\mathsf{StMod}(k G)$ into $\mathsf{KInj}(k G)$, taking a module $M$ to a Tate resolution $\mathsf{t}M$ of $M$.
nodes.name: Tate resolution embedding

nodes.statement: This sits in a recollement \[ \xymatrix{\mathsf{StMod}(k G)\simeq\mathsf{K^{ac}Inj}(k G)\ar[r] & \mathsf{KInj}(k G) \ar@<1ex>[l]\ar@<-1ex>[l]\ar[r] & \mathsf{D}(k G)\ar@<1ex>[l]\ar@<-1ex>[l]} \] where $\mathsf{K^{ac}Inj}(k G)$ is the full subcategory of acyclic complexes, and $\mathsf{D}(k G)$ is the derived category.
nodes.name: Recollement StMod - KInj - D(kG)

nodes.statement: The left adjoints in this recollement preserve compactness and give us functors on compact objects \[ \mathsf{stmod}(k G) \leftarrow \mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G) \leftarrow \mathsf{Perf}(k G) \] where $\mathsf{Perf}(k G)$ consists of the perfect complexes.
nodes.name: Functors on compact objects

nodes.statement: This gives Rickard's equivalence \[ \mathsf{stmod}(k G)\simeq\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)/\mathsf{Perf}(k G), \] see Theorem~2.1 of~\cite{Rickard:1989a}.
nodes.name: Rickard's equivalence
conclusions: \[ \mathsf{stmod}(k G)\simeq\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)/\mathsf{Perf}(k G), \]

nodes.statement: Given any object $X$ in $\mathsf{KInj}(k G)$, the left adjoints give a triangle \[ \mathsf{pk} \otimes X \to X \to \mathsf{tk} \otimes X \to \Sigma\mathsf{pk}\otimes X \] while the right adjoints give a triangle \[ \mathsf{Hom}(\mathsf{tk},X) \to X \to \mathsf{Hom}(\mathsf{pk},X) \to \Sigma\mathsf{Hom}(\mathsf{tk},X). \]
nodes.name: Tate and Hom triangles

nodes.statement: If $C$ is in $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)\subseteq\mathsf{KInj}(k G)$ then for all $X$ in $\mathsf{KInj}(k G)$ we have \[ \mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(X,\mathsf{pk}\otimes C) \cong \mathsf{Hom}_k(\mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(C,X),k). \]
nodes.name: Tate duality in KInj(kG)
conclusions: \[ \mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(X,\mathsf{pk}\otimes C) \cong \mathsf{Hom}_k(\mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(C,X),k). \]
nodes.label: pr:Tate-KInj

nodes.statement: It follows from Tate duality that the Brown--Comenetz dual is given by \[ X^*= \mathsf{Hom}(X,\mathsf{pk}) \cong \mathsf{Hom}_{k}(X,k) \] where $\mathsf{pk}$ is a projective resolution of $k$, while the Spanier--Whitehead dual is given by \[ X^\vee = \mathsf{Hom}(X,\mathsf{ik}). \]
nodes.name: Brown–Comenetz and Spanier–Whitehead duals in KInj(kG)

nodes.statement: If we take the vector space dual of a Tate resolution of a $k G$-module $M$, we get a Tate resolution of the Brown--Comenetz dual $M^*=\Omega\mathsf{Hom}_{k}(M,k)$, which is a shift of a Tate resolution of the Spanier--Whitehead dual $M^\vee=\mathsf{Hom}_k(M,k)$. This explains the shift in numbering between Tate duality in $\mathsf{StMod}(k G)$ and in $\mathsf{KInj}(k G)$ (compare Proposition~\ref{pr:Tate-StMod} with Proposition~\ref{pr:Tate-KInj}).
nodes.name: Shift between the two Tate dualities
nodes.statement_short: Dualizing a Tate resolution gives the Brown–Comenetz dual, a shift of the Spanier–Whitehead dual, explaining the index shift.

nodes.statement: The category $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$ is generated by the simple $k G$-modules. It is also generated by the permutation module $k(G/S)$ on the cosets of a Sylow $p$-subgroup $S$.
nodes.name: Generators of D^b(kG)
conclusions: The category $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$ is generated by the simple $k G$-modules.
It is also generated by the permutation module $k(G/S)$ on the cosets of a Sylow $p$-subgroup $S$.
nodes.label: le:kG/S-gen

nodes.statement: Generation by the simple modules follows from the fact that every finitely generated module has a finite filtration with simple filtered quotients. In particular, for a $p$-group $S$, $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k S)$ is generated by $k$. For a general finite group, given an object $X$ in $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$, the restriction $\mathop{\rm res}_{G,S}(X)$ is generated by $k$, and so inducing back up to $G$, the module $\mathop{\rm ind}_{S,G}\mathop{\rm res}_{G,S}(X)$ is generated by $\mathop{\rm ind}_{S,G}(k)=k(G/S)$. The second statement now follows from the fact that $X$ is isomorphic to a direct summand of $\mathop{\rm ind}_{S,G}\mathop{\rm res}_{G,S}(X)$.
nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.28
nodes.statement_short: Filtrations by simples; for the second part restrict to a Sylow subgroup and induce back, using that $X$ is a summand of ind res $X$.

nodes.name: Composition series
nodes.statement_short: Filtrations by simples give generation; for a $p$-group, by $k$.

nodes.statement: For a general finite group, given an object $X$ in $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$, the restriction $\mathop{\rm res}_{G,S}(X)$ is generated by $k$, and so inducing back up to $G$, the module $\mathop{\rm ind}_{S,G}\mathop{\rm res}_{G,S}(X)$ is generated by $\mathop{\rm ind}_{S,G}(k)=k(G/S)$.
nodes.name: Restrict and induce
nodes.statement_short: ind res $X$ is generated by $k(G/S)$.

nodes.statement: The second statement now follows from the fact that $X$ is isomorphic to a direct summand of $\mathop{\rm ind}_{S,G}\mathop{\rm res}_{G,S}(X)$.
nodes.name: Summand argument
nodes.statement_short: $X$ is a summand of ind res $X$.

nodes.statement: We have $\mathsf{ik}^\perp={}^\perp\mathsf{ik}=\mathsf{KInj}^0(k G)$, the no cohomology objects in $\mathsf{KInj}(k G)$.
nodes.name: No cohomology objects are the perp of ik
conclusions: $\mathsf{ik}^\perp={}^\perp\mathsf{ik}=\mathsf{KInj}^0(k G)$

nodes.statement: We have a recollement of triangulated categories \[ \xymatrix{\mathsf{KInj}^0(k G) \ar[r]|u & \mathsf{KInj}(k G) \ar[r]|(0.37)v\ar@<1ex>[l]^{u_\lambda}\ar@<-1ex>[l]_{u_\rho} & \mathsf{KInj}(k G)/\mathsf{KInj}^0(k G) \ar@<1ex>[l]^(0.63){v_\lambda} \ar@<-1ex>[l]_(0.63){v_\rho}} \] where the right hand side is the Verdier quotient.
nodes.name: Recollement for KInj^0(kG) in KInj(kG)

nodes.statement: The image of the right adjoint $v_\rho$ is the localising subcategory $\mathsf{Loc}(\mathsf{ik})$ of $\mathsf{KInj}(k G)$ generated by $\mathsf{ik}$, while the image of the left adjoint $v_\lambda$ is the colocalising subcategory $\mathsf{Coloc}(\mathsf{ik})$ cogenerated by $\mathsf{ik}$.
nodes.name: Loc(ik) and Coloc(ik) as images of the adjoints

nodes.statement: Given an object $X$ in $\mathsf{KInj}(k G)$, this gives us a localisation triangle \[ v_\rho v X \to X \to u_\rho u X \to \Sigma v_\rho v X \] where $v_\rho v X$ is in $\mathsf{Loc}(\mathsf{ik})$, $v_\rho v X \to X$ is a cohomology equivalence and $u_\rho u X$ is in $\mathsf{KInj}^0(k G)$.
nodes.name: Localisation triangle
conclusions: $v_\rho v X$ is in $\mathsf{Loc}(\mathsf{ik})$, $v_\rho v X \to X$ is a cohomology equivalence and $u_\rho u X$ is in $\mathsf{KInj}^0(k G)$

nodes.statement: Similarly, it gives us a colocalisation triangle \[ u_\lambda u X \to X \to v_\lambda v X \to \Sigma u_\lambda u X \] where $v_\lambda v X$ is in $\mathsf{Coloc}(\mathsf{ik})$, $X \to v_\lambda v X$ is a cohomology equivalence and $u_\lambda u X$ is in $\mathsf{KInj}^0(k G)$.
nodes.name: Colocalisation triangle
conclusions: $v_\lambda v X$ is in $\mathsf{Coloc}(\mathsf{ik})$, $X \to v_\lambda v X$ is a cohomology equivalence and $u_\lambda u X$ is in $\mathsf{KInj}^0(k G)$

nodes.statement: We define $\mathsf{KInj}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$ to be the thick subcategory of $\mathsf{KInj}(k G)$ consisting of objects $X$ whose cohomology $H^*(G,X)$ is finitely generated as a module over $H^*(G,k)$. Thus $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)\subseteq\mathsf{KInj}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$ and $\mathsf{KInj}^0(k G)\subseteq\mathsf{KInj}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$. We define $\mathsf{Loc}^{\mathsf b}(\mathsf{ik})$ to be the thick subcategory $\mathsf{Loc}(\mathsf{ik})\cap \mathsf{KInj}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)\subseteq\mathsf{KInj}(k G)$. So $v_\rho$ induces an equivalence \begin{equation} \mathsf{KInj}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)/\mathsf{KInj}^0(k G)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathsf{Loc}^{\mathsf b}(\mathsf{ik}). \end{equation}
nodes.name: KInj^b(kG) and Loc^b(ik)
differentia: objects $X$ whose cohomology $H^*(G,X)$ is finitely generated as a module over $H^*(G,k)$
nodes.statement_short: KInj^b(kG): objects with finitely generated cohomology; Loc^b(ik) its intersection with Loc(ik), equivalent to KInj^b/KInj^0.
also_stated_at: We write $\mathsf{KInj}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$ for the thick subcategory of objects such that $H^*(G,X)$ is finitely generated as a module over $H^*(G,k)$.

nodes.statement: \mathsf{KInj}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)/\mathsf{KInj}^0(k G)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathsf{Loc}^{\mathsf b}(\mathsf{ik}).
nodes.name: Equivalence KInj^b/KInj^0 = Loc^b(ik)
nodes.label: eq:KInjb/KInj0

nodes.statement: Suppose that $G$ is a finite $p$-group. Then $\mathsf{KInj}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)=\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$.
nodes.name: KInj^b = D^b for p-groups
conclusions: $\mathsf{KInj}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)=\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$
nodes.label: th:Kinjb-pgroup

nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an object in $\mathsf{KInj}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$. Thinking of $H^*(G,X)$ as $\mathsf{Hom}_{\mathsf{KInj}(k G)}(\mathsf{ik},X)$, it follows from the hypothesis that if $Y$ is in $\mathsf{Thick}(\mathsf{ik})$ then $\mathsf{Hom}_{\mathsf{KInj}(k G)}(Y,X)$ is finitely generated as a module over $H^*(G,k)$. In the case of a finite $p$-group, the module $k G$, regarded as an element of $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$ concentrated in a single degree, is in $\mathsf{Thick}(\mathsf{ik})$, as it is built from $|G|$ copies of $k$. So $\mathsf{Hom}_{\mathsf{KInj}(k G)}(k G,X)$ is finitely generated. But it is also killed by the ideal of positive (cohomological) degree elements, so it is finite dimensional. But $\mathsf{Hom}_{\mathsf{KInj}(k G)}(k G,X)$ is the cohomology of $X$ as a complex. So $X$ is exact in all but finitely many degrees, and is hence equivalent to a semi-injective resolution of an object in $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$.
nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.30
nodes.statement_short: For a $p$-group $kG$ lies in Thick(ik), so the ordinary cohomology of $X$ is finitely generated and killed by positive degrees, hence finite.

nodes.statement: Suppose that $X$ is an object in $\mathsf{KInj}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$. Thinking of $H^*(G,X)$ as $\mathsf{Hom}_{\mathsf{KInj}(k G)}(\mathsf{ik},X)$, it follows from the hypothesis that if $Y$ is in $\mathsf{Thick}(\mathsf{ik})$ then $\mathsf{Hom}_{\mathsf{KInj}(k G)}(Y,X)$ is finitely generated as a module over $H^*(G,k)$.
nodes.name: Hom from Thick(ik) is finitely generated
nodes.statement_short: Hom from any object of Thick(ik) into $X$ is finitely generated.

nodes.statement: In the case of a finite $p$-group, the module $k G$, regarded as an element of $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$ concentrated in a single degree, is in $\mathsf{Thick}(\mathsf{ik})$, as it is built from $|G|$ copies of $k$. So $\mathsf{Hom}_{\mathsf{KInj}(k G)}(k G,X)$ is finitely generated.
nodes.name: kG lies in Thick(ik)
nodes.statement_short: For a $p$-group $kG$ is built from copies of $k$, so Hom$(kG,X)$ is finitely generated.

nodes.statement: But it is also killed by the ideal of positive (cohomological) degree elements, so it is finite dimensional.
nodes.name: Finite dimensional
nodes.statement_short: Killed by positive degree elements, so finite dimensional.

nodes.statement: But $\mathsf{Hom}_{\mathsf{KInj}(k G)}(k G,X)$ is the cohomology of $X$ as a complex. So $X$ is exact in all but finitely many degrees, and is hence equivalent to a semi-injective resolution of an object in $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$.
nodes.name: X has bounded cohomology
nodes.statement_short: This is the cohomology of $X$, so $X$ is in D^b(kG).

nodes.statement: Given a complex $X$ in $\mathsf{KInj}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$ there is a subcomplex $Y$ such that the inclusion $Y\to X$ is a cohomology equivalence, and such that $Y$ is zero in all sufficiently large negative (cohomological) degrees, and finite dimensional in all degrees.
nodes.name: Whittling down to a finite-type subcomplex
conclusions: there is a subcomplex $Y$ such that the inclusion $Y\to X$ is a cohomology equivalence, and such that $Y$ is zero in all sufficiently large negative (cohomological) degrees, and finite dimensional in all degrees
nodes.label: pr:whittle-down

nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an object in $\mathsf{KInj}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$. Since $H^*(G,X)$ is finitely generated over $H^*(G,k)$, there exists $n\in \mathbb Z$ such that $H^i(G,X)=0$ for $i< n$. Assuming without loss of generality that $X$ is minimal, we have $\mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(k,X^i)=0$ for $i< n$. Then the (brutal) truncation $X^{< n}$ is in $\mathsf{KInj}^0(k G)$, and the inclusion $X^{\geqslant n}\to X$ is a cohomology equivalence. We may now assume that $X^i=0$ for $i<n$. Then there is a finite dimensional summand $Y^n$ of $X^n$ such that the inclusion induces an isomorphism $\mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(k,Y^n) \to \mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(k,X^n)$. Next, there is a finite dimensional summand $Y^{n+1}$ of $X^{n+1}$ which contains the image of $Y^n$ under the differential, and such that $\mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(k,Y^{n+1}) \to \mathsf{Hom}_{k G}(k,X^{n+1})$ is an isomorphism. nodes.statement: We begin by showing that Conjecture~\ref{conj:strong-stmod} implies Conjecture~\ref{conj:strong-Db} and Conjecture~\ref{conj:weak-stmod} implies Conjecture~\ref{conj:weak-Db}. Let $X$ be an object in $\mathsf{KInj}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$. Replacing $X$ by the cohomologically equivalent $v_\rho v X$, which we may do in both Conjecture~\ref{conj:strong-Db} and Conjecture~\ref{conj:weak-Db}, we may suppose that $X$ is in $\mathsf{Loc}(\mathsf{ik})$. Using Proposition~\ref{pr:whittle-down} and shifting if necessary we may assume that $X^n=0$ for $n<0$. By Corollary~\ref{co:tX}, $\mathsf{tk} \otimes X$ is a Tate resolution of a $k G$-module $M$ in $\mathsf{StMod}^b(k G)\cap \mathsf{Loc}(\mathsf{ik})$. If Conjecture~\ref{conj:strong-stmod} holds, there is a finitely generated $k G$-module $M'\in \mathsf{stmod}(k G)$ such that $M\to M'$ is a cohomology equivalence; whereas if Conjecture~\ref{conj:weak-stmod} holds then $M$ is a module in $\mathsf{Thick}(\mathsf{stmod}(k G),\mathsf{StMod}^0(k G))$, and we set $M'=M$. The module $M'$ is only well defined up to adding and removing projective summands, but we regard it as an object in $\mathsf{Mod}(k G)$. Then the complex $\mathsf{ik} \otimes M'$ is an injective resolution of $M'$, and may be regarded as an object in $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)\subseteq\mathsf{KInj}(k G)$, respectively $\mathsf{Thick}(\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G),\mathsf{KInj}^0(k G))$, giving us a diagram \[ \xymatrix@=6mm{\mathsf{pk} \otimes X \ar[r] & X \ar[r]\ar@{.>}[d] & \mathsf{tk}\otimes X = \mathsf{t}M\ar[d] \\ &\mathsf{ik} \otimes M' \ar[r]& \mathsf{tk} \otimes M' \ar[r] & \Sigma \mathsf{pk} \otimes M'.} \] Since $X^n=0$ for $n<0$, and $(\Sigma\mathsf{pk}\otimes M')^n=0$ for $n\geqslant 0$, there are no no-zero maps from $X$ to $\Sigma \mathsf{pk} \otimes M'$. So we can fill in the dotted arrow to make the diagram above commutative. This dotted arrow is an isomorphism in cohomology in sufficiently large degrees. Complete this to a triangle \[ Y \to X \to \mathsf{ik}\otimes M' \to \Sigma Y. \] Then $Y$ has cohomology only in finitely many degrees, and is in $\mathsf{Loc}(\mathsf{ik})$, so it is in $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$. Since $\mathsf{ik} \otimes M'$ is in $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$, respectively $\mathsf{Thick}(\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G),\mathsf{KInj}^0(k G))$ it follows that $X$ is. This completes the proof that Conjecture~\ref{conj:strong-stmod} implies Conjecture~\ref{conj:strong-Db} and that Conjecture~\ref{conj:weak-stmod} imples Conjecture~\ref{conj:weak-Db}. Conversely, let $M$ be a module in $\mathsf{StMod}^b(k G)$. We may suppose that $M$ has no projective summands. Then $\mathsf{ik} \otimes M$ is an object in $\mathsf{KInj}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$. If Conjecture~\ref{conj:strong-Db} holds, then there is an object $X$ in $\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G)$ that is cohomology equivalent to $\mathsf{ik}\otimes M$; whereas if Conjecture~\ref{conj:weak-Db} holds, then $\mathsf{ik}\otimes M$ is in $\mathsf{Thick}(\mathsf{D}^{\mathsf{b}}(k G),\mathsf{KInj}^0(k G))$, and we set $X=\mathsf{ik}\otimes M$. Then $\mathsf{tk}\otimes X$ is in $\mathsf{stmod}(k G)$, respectively $\mathsf{Thick}(\mathsf{stmod}(k G),\mathsf{StMod}^0(k G))$, and is cohomology equivalent to $M$.

This group regularly permutes the connected components of $\Omega BG{}^{^\wedge}_p$, and the connected component of the identity is $\Omega BO^p(G){}^{^\wedge}_p$. So we may assume without loss of generality that $G=O^p(G)$, so that \[ \pi_0\Omega BG{}^{^\wedge}_p=\pi_1 BG{}^{^\wedge}_p=G/O^pG=1. \] Now choose an embedding $G\to SU(n)$, and consider the fibre sequence \[ \Omega BG{}^{^\wedge}_p \to SU(n){}^{^\wedge}_p \to (SU(n)/G){}^{^\wedge}_p \to BG{}^{^\wedge}_p \to BSU(n){}^{^\wedge}_p. \] We have $\pi_1(SU(n)/G){}^{^\wedge}_p=1$, and so in the spectral sequence \[ H^*((SU(n)/G){}^{^\wedge}_p,H^*(\Omega BG{}^{^\wedge}_p)) \Rightarrow H^*(SU(n){}^{^\wedge}_p), \] the $E_2$ page is a tensor product.
